::: {.solutions}

Here is an uncomfortable fact: you have done mathematics for ten years, and nobody has ever told you what
**"only if"** means. You have used it, you have read it in questions, and you almost certainly think it
means the same as "if". It does not — it means the **opposite direction**. The TMUA knows that, which is
why *only if* appears on every recent Paper 2.

The good news is that there is no algebra here. It is a small number of precise distinctions, and once you
have them a whole category of Paper 2 questions becomes nearly free. Every question below is answered by
the same move: **rewrite the sentence as "if … then …", then read off which way the arrow points.**

Specification: **Arg1** — *true and false; and, or (inclusive), not; statements of the form* **if A then B**,
**A if B**, **A only if B**, **A if and only if B**. Official source: **Notes on Logic and Proof**, pp. 24–34.

---

# Part 1 — Easy

Single-idea warm-ups. Get the vocabulary automatic here, because every harder question is built out of it.

## Question 1

::: {.question}
Let $n = 21$. For each of the following, state whether it is **true** or **false**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $n$ is divisible by $3$ **and** $n$ is divisible by $6$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $n$ is divisible by $3$ **or** $n$ is divisible by $6$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) $n$ is **not** divisible by $6$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) $n$ is divisible by $3$ **or** $n$ is divisible by $7$. **[1]**
:::

Start by settling the two facts everything rests on: $21 = 3 \times 7$, so it **is** divisible by $3$ and
by $7$, and it is **not** divisible by $6$. Then the only thing being tested is what each connective
demands — and the one to watch is *or*, because [in mathematics "or" is **inclusive**]{.hl}: it is
satisfied when one side holds, and also when both do.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — statements; the connectives *and*, *or*, *not*
:::


$21 = 3 \times 7$. So "divisible by $3$" is **true**, "divisible by $7$" is **true**, and "divisible by
$6$" is **false** (a multiple of $6$ must be even, and $21$ is odd).

**(a) False.** *And* needs **both** sides true; the second is false.

**(b) True.** *Or* needs **at least one** side true, and the first is true. The second being false does
not matter.

**(c) True.** *Not* flips a false statement into a true one.

**(d) True.** Both sides happen to be true — and [that is still fine for "or"]{.hl}. Inclusive *or* is
satisfied by "one, the other, or both".

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (d) marked false because "both are true, so it can't be *or*" | This is the exclusive-*or* of everyday English ("tea or coffee"). **Mathematics never means that** — "or" always allows both. |
| (a) marked true because $21$ is divisible by $3$ | *And* is only true when **both** halves are true. One good half is not enough. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — statements and the three connectives

A **statement** is a sentence that is either **true or false** — definitely one or the other. Nothing
else counts, and Paper 2 is built entirely out of them, so it is worth being able to spot one instantly.

**These are statements** (each has a definite truth value, even if you don't know it yet):

| Statement | True or false? |
|---|---|
| $21$ is divisible by $3$ | true |
| $21$ is divisible by $6$ | false |
| $7$ is prime | true |
| Every even number greater than $2$ is the sum of two primes | *nobody knows* — but it is still **either** true or false, so it **is** a statement |

**These are NOT statements:**

| Not a statement | Why |
|---|---|
| $x$ is divisible by $3$ | No truth value until you say what $x$ is. It is true for $x=6$, false for $x=7$. |
| $x + 1$ | Not even a sentence — it is an *expression*, a thing, not a claim about a thing. |
| Is $21$ prime? | A **question**. Questions cannot be true or false. |
| Solve the equation. | An **instruction**. Same reason. |
| $21$ is a large number | **Vague** — "large" is not defined, so there is no definite answer. |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The test:** could you, in principle, put the word *"It is true that …"* in front of the sentence and
have it make sense? If yes, it is a statement.

**The one that surprises people** is the fourth row of the first table. A statement does **not** have to
be a sentence *you* can settle — it only has to *have* an answer. That is why unsolved conjectures are
perfectly good statements.

**And note the third row of the second table:** *"$x$ is divisible by $3$"* becomes a statement the moment
you either fix $x$ ("$x=6$") or put a quantifier in front of it ("**for all** $x$ …", "**there exists** an
$x$ such that …"). That is Session 4 — but it is why the specification treats quantifiers as part of the
same topic.
:::

Everything on Paper 2 is built by gluing statements together, and there are exactly three glues:

| Connective | True exactly when | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| **not $A$** | $A$ is false | — |
| **$A$ and $B$** | **both** are true | one true half is not enough |
| **$A$ or $B$** | **at least one** is true | **includes the case where both are true** |

**The one that catches people is *or*.** In ordinary English "tea or coffee" means one *but not both* —
that is *exclusive* or. Mathematics always uses **inclusive** or: "$x>0$ or $x$ is an integer" is true for
$x=5$, where both hold.

The specification says you will **not** be asked to use symbols ($\land$, $\lor$, $\Rightarrow$) or to
complete formal truth tables. It is all tested in English sentences — which is reassuring, but it also
means you cannot hide behind notation.
:::

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Assume the following statement is **true**:

> *If it is Sunday, then the church bells ring.*

In each case, state what you can conclude — or write "nothing".

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) You know it **is** Sunday. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) You know it is **not** Sunday. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) You hear the bells **ringing**. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) You notice the bells are **silent**. **[1]**
:::

This is the single most important question on the page, and the two "nothing" answers are the lesson. An
if-statement is [a one-way promise]{.hl}: it tells you what follows *when the front half holds*, and says
nothing at all when it doesn't. Before answering (c), ask yourself honestly whether bells could ring on a
Tuesday — nothing in the sentence forbids it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — what "if $A$ then $B$" does, and does not, tell you
:::


**(a) The bells ring.** That is exactly what the statement promises.

**(b) Nothing.** The statement says nothing about Tuesdays or Wednesdays. The bells might ring for a
wedding; they might not. [Knowing the front half is false tells you nothing.]{.hl}

**(c) Nothing.** Hearing bells does **not** mean it is Sunday — they could be ringing for any other
reason. This is the direction people get wrong.

**(d) It is not Sunday.** If it *were* Sunday, the bells would have rung. Silence therefore rules Sunday
out. [Denying the back half denies the front half.]{.hl}

$\blacksquare$

Collecting it into a table — this table *is* the topic:

| What you know | What you can conclude |
|---|---|
| It **is** Sunday | The bells ring |
| It is **not** Sunday | **Nothing** |
| The bells **ring** | **Nothing** |
| The bells are **silent** | It is **not** Sunday |

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (c) "So it must be Sunday" | That is running the arrow backwards. Bells ringing is consistent with any day. |
| (b) "So the bells don't ring" | The statement never covers non-Sundays. It is silent, so you must be too. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — implication is a one-way promise

**First, the word itself.** An **implication** is any statement of the form

$$A \Rightarrow B \qquad \text{read aloud as } \textbf{“} A \textbf{ implies } B \textbf{”} \text{ or } \textbf{“if } A \textbf{, then } B \textbf{”.}$$

It is built from two smaller statements joined by an arrow, and it is itself a statement — it is true or
false as a whole. The two halves have names worth knowing, because questions refer to them:

| Part | Name | In $A \Rightarrow B$ |
|---|---|---|
| the front half | **hypothesis** (or *antecedent*) | $A$ |
| the back half | **conclusion** (or *consequent*) | $B$ |

So "write it as an implication" simply means **"write it with an arrow"** — decide which half is the
hypothesis and which is the conclusion, and point the arrow from the first to the second.

Here $A$ = *it is Sunday* and $B$ = *the bells ring*, so the statement is $A \Rightarrow B$.

**The one thing to hold on to:** $A \Rightarrow B$ says *every* $A$-case is also a $B$-case. Picture $A$ as
a circle sitting **inside** a bigger circle $B$. Then:

- Inside $A$ ⟹ certainly inside $B$. ✓ (row 1)
- Outside $A$ ⟹ could be anywhere. (row 2 — nothing)
- Inside $B$ ⟹ could be in the $A$ part or the outer ring. (row 3 — nothing)
- Outside $B$ ⟹ certainly outside $A$, since all of $A$ is inside $B$. ✓ (row 4)

Rows 1 and 4 are the two things you may deduce; rows 2 and 3 are the two traps.

**Rows 3 and 4 each have a name, and they are easy to mix up.**

| Row | Name | Form | Same as the original? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Row 4** | **contrapositive** | not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$ &nbsp;*(negate **and** reverse)* | **Yes, always** |
| **Row 3** | **converse** | $B \Rightarrow A$ &nbsp;*(reverse only)* | **No** — a different statement, usually false |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Do not confuse these two words.** It is the **contrapositive** that is always equivalent to the
original, never the **converse**. Getting the two labels the wrong way round is the single most expensive
mistake in this whole topic, because every Paper 2 "which of these is equivalent?" question turns on it.

A one-second check: the contrapositive has **negations in it**; the converse does **not**.
:::

Test it on the bells. Original: *if it is Sunday, the bells ring.*

- **Contrapositive**: *if the bells do not ring, it is not Sunday.* — Clearly says the same thing. ✓
- **Converse**: *if the bells ring, it is Sunday.* — A different claim, and a false one (weddings). ✗

Those are Session 2 in full; for now just hold on to the fact that **one direction is free and the other
has to be earned**.

A concrete pair to keep in your head:

$$x = 3 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 = 9 \quad \text{(true)}, \qquad\qquad x^2 = 9 \;\not\Rightarrow\; x = 3 \quad (x = -3).$$
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Decide whether each statement is **true** or **false**, and give a
counterexample for each false one.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $n$ is divisible by $6$ **only if** $n$ is divisible by $3$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $n$ is divisible by $6$ **if** $n$ is divisible by $3$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) $n$ is divisible by $3$ **only if** $n$ is divisible by $6$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) $n$ is divisible by $6$ **if and only if** $n$ is divisible by $2$ **and** by $3$. **[2]**
:::

Do not reason about these in English — [rewrite each one as "if … then …" first]{.hl}, then check it. Two
rules do all the work: **"only if" keeps the order** ($A$ only if $B$ means if $A$ then $B$), while a bare
**"if" swaps it** ($A$ if $B$ means if $B$ then $A$). Notice (a) and (c) use the identical words with
"only if" moved — so if the rules are right, one of them should come out true and the other false.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — the four statement forms; deciding true or false
:::


**(a) True.** Rewrite: *if $n$ is divisible by $6$, then $n$ is divisible by $3$.* Every multiple of $6$ is
$6k = 3(2k)$, so yes.

**(b) False.** Bare "if", so **swap**: *if $n$ is divisible by $3$, then $n$ is divisible by $6$.*
Counterexample $n = 9$: divisible by $3$, not by $6$.

**(c) False.** Rewrite: *if $n$ is divisible by $3$, then $n$ is divisible by $6$.* This is the **same
statement as (b)**, so the same counterexample $n=9$ works.

*Compare (a) and (c): identical words, "only if" attached to the other half, and the truth value flips.
That is the whole point of the question.*

**(d) True.** Both directions hold, so "if and only if" is earned:

- ($\Rightarrow$) If $6$ divides $n$ then $n = 6k = 2(3k) = 3(2k)$, so $2$ divides $n$ and $3$ divides $n$. ✓
- ($\Leftarrow$) If $2$ divides $n$ and $3$ divides $n$, then since $2$ and $3$ share no factor, $6$ divides $n$. ✓

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Reading (a) and (c) as the same statement | They are opposites. "Only if" marks **which half gets forced**, and it has moved. |
| Treating "$A$ if $B$" as $A \Rightarrow B$ | The bare **"if" introduces the forcer**: it is $B \Rightarrow A$. |
| Proving only one direction in (d) and stopping | "If and only if" is **two** claims. Prove both, or say which one you have. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the four forms (the table to memorise)

| The English | Means | In words |
|---|---|---|
| **if $A$ then $B$** | $A \Rightarrow B$ | $A$ forces $B$ |
| **$A$ if $B$** | $B \Rightarrow A$ | the arrow points **backwards** |
| **$A$ only if $B$** | $A \Rightarrow B$ | **same as "if $A$ then $B$"** |
| **$A$ if and only if $B$** | $A \Leftrightarrow B$ | both directions at once |

Two facts generate the whole table:

1. **The bare "if" introduces the thing that does the forcing.** Whatever follows the word *if* sits at the
   *front* of the arrow. So "$A$ **if** $B$" is $B \Rightarrow A$.
2. **"Only if" introduces the thing that gets forced.** So "$A$ **only if** $B$" is $A \Rightarrow B$.

Which means **"$A$ if $B$" and "$A$ only if $B$" are opposite statements, differing by two letters.**

**Why does "only if" work that way?** Read it as the Notes do: *"the bells ring **only if** it is Sunday"*
says *Sunday is the only circumstance in which the bells ring* — so hearing bells forces it to be Sunday.
Note also what it does **not** promise: the bells might be broken on some Sunday. "Only if" gives a
**restriction**, not a guarantee.

**"If and only if" is two statements in one coat:**

$$A \text{ iff } B \;\equiv\; (A \text{ if } B) \textbf{ and } (A \text{ only if } B) \;\equiv\; (B \Rightarrow A) \textbf{ and } (A \Rightarrow B).$$

So it must be **earned twice**. Proving one direction and declaring victory is the classic way to lose a
Paper 2 mark.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The method, every time.** Don't think — **rewrite as "if … then …" first**, then read the arrow.
:::
:::

# Part 2 — Medium

Now the same rules under a bit of pressure: several statements at once, and wording that fights you.

## Question 4

::: {.question}
$P$ and $Q$ are statements. Write each of the following as an implication, using $\Rightarrow$ between
$P$ and $Q$ (or $\Leftrightarrow$ where appropriate).

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $P$ only if $Q$ **[1]** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; (b) $P$ if $Q$ **[1]** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
(c) $Q$ only if $P$ **[1]** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; (d) $Q$ if and only if $P$ **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(e) Hence state which **two** of (a)–(d) say the same thing as each other. **[1]**
:::

This is pure mechanics, and it is worth drilling until it takes no thought at all — in the exam you will be
doing this while also holding the actual mathematics in your head. Work strictly by the two rules and
[resist the urge to reason about meaning]{.hl}; meaning is what makes people flip arrows by accident.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — translating "only if" and "if" into arrows, at speed
:::


**(a)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp;— "only if" keeps the order.

**(b)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp;— bare "if" introduces the forcer, so the arrow starts at $Q$.

**(c)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp;— "only if" again keeps the order, but the halves have been swapped
around, so the arrow now starts at $Q$.

**(d)** $Q \Leftrightarrow P$, which is the same as $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ — [an "if and only if" reads the
same in both directions]{.hl}, so the order does not matter here.

**(e)** **(b) and (c)** are the same statement: both are $Q \Rightarrow P$.

$\blacksquare$

That last part is the point of the question. *"$P$ if $Q$"* and *"$Q$ only if $P$"* look completely
different in English and mean exactly the same thing.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (c) written as $P \Rightarrow Q$ | Apply the rule to the sentence *as written*: "**$Q$** only if $P$" forces $Q$ first, so $Q \Rightarrow P$. |
| Thinking (a) and (b) are the same | They are exact opposites — the commonest error in this whole topic. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — a mechanical routine

When a sentence contains *if* or *only if*:

1. **Find the connective** — is it a bare *if*, an *only if*, or an *if and only if*?
2. **Apply the rule.**
   - *only if* → arrow runs **left to right** as written: "$X$ only if $Y$" is $X \Rightarrow Y$.
   - bare *if* → arrow runs **right to left**: "$X$ if $Y$" is $Y \Rightarrow X$.
   - *if and only if* → **both** arrows; order irrelevant.
3. **Re-read your arrow as "if … then …"** and check it sounds like the original sentence.

The four English forms collapse to only **three** distinct meanings, which is why pairs of very different
looking sentences turn out to be identical:

$$\underbrace{\text{if } P \text{ then } Q \;=\; P \text{ only if } Q \;=\; Q \text{ if } P}_{P \,\Rightarrow\, Q}, \qquad
\underbrace{\text{if } Q \text{ then } P \;=\; Q \text{ only if } P \;=\; P \text{ if } Q}_{Q \,\Rightarrow\, P}, \qquad
\underbrace{P \text{ iff } Q}_{P \,\Leftrightarrow\, Q}$$

Being able to see at a glance which of the three boxes a sentence lands in is exactly what Paper 2 tests.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**About the abbreviation "iff".** Yes — **iff** is simply short for **"if and only if"**. The doubled *f*
is deliberate, not a typo: *if* means one direction, *iff* means both.

$$P \text{ iff } Q \qquad \equiv \qquad P \text{ if and only if } Q \qquad \equiv \qquad P \Leftrightarrow Q$$

Two practical notes:

- **Read it aloud as "if and only if"**, never as the sound "iff". It is a written shorthand only.
- It will **not** appear on the TMUA paper itself — the test writes the words out in full. But it appears
  constantly in textbooks and in these notes, so you need to recognise it.

The three ways of writing the same thing — *iff*, *if and only if*, and $\Leftrightarrow$ — are
interchangeable. The symbol $\Leftrightarrow$ is a double-headed arrow precisely because the statement
runs both ways.
:::
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
For a positive integer $n$, consider the statement

> $n$ is prime **only if** $n$ has exactly two positive factors.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Rewrite the statement in the form "if … then …". **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Assuming the statement is true, what can you conclude about $n$ if you are told that $n$
has exactly two positive factors? **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Now consider instead: *$n$ is prime **if** $n$ has exactly two positive factors.*
Is this the same statement as the original? Justify your answer. **[2]**
:::

Part (b) is the trap, and it is worth slowing down for: you are being handed the **back** half of the
implication and asked what follows. Recall from Question 2 that this is precisely the case where the honest
answer is *nothing*. Part (c) then asks you to compare the two directions — and here something unusual
happens, because [both directions are actually true for this particular pair of statements]{.hl}, which is
not the same as the two *sentences* meaning the same thing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — reading an "only if" statement in context; what does and does not follow
:::


**(a)** "Only if" keeps the order:

> *If $n$ is prime, then $n$ has exactly two positive factors.*

**(b)** **Nothing follows** from the original statement alone. You have been given the *conclusion*, and an
implication run backwards proves nothing — this is exactly row 3 of the church-bells table.

*(It is of course a true fact about integers that having exactly two factors makes $n$ prime — but that is
extra knowledge, **not** something the given statement licenses.)*

**(c)** **No, it is a different statement**, though it also happens to be true. The bare "if" swaps the
arrow:

$$\text{original: } (n \text{ prime}) \Rightarrow (n \text{ has exactly two factors})$$
$$\text{new: } (n \text{ has exactly two factors}) \Rightarrow (n \text{ prime})$$

These are **converses** of each other — *reversed, with nothing negated*. Both happen to be true here,
which is precisely why "$n$ is prime **if and only if** $n$ has exactly two positive factors" is a correct
definition of primality. But [being both true is a coincidence of this example, not a rule]{.hl}: for
*$x=3$* and *$x^2=9$*, only one direction holds.

*(Careful: a converse is **not** a contrapositive. The contrapositive of the original would be "if $n$ does
**not** have exactly two positive factors, then $n$ is **not** prime" — negated as well as reversed, and
therefore automatically true whenever the original is.)*

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (b) "Then $n$ is prime" | True in real life, but **not deducible from the statement given**. Paper 2 asks what *follows*, not what you happen to know. |
| (c) "Same statement, because both are true" | Two statements can both be true without being the *same* statement. Compare the arrows, not the truth values. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — "the same statement" vs "both true"

This is a distinction Paper 2 leans on repeatedly.

- Two statements are **equivalent** when they are true in *exactly the same circumstances* — every case,
  not just the one in front of you.
- Two statements can **both be true** while being completely different claims.

$P \Rightarrow Q$ and $Q \Rightarrow P$ are **never** automatically equivalent. Sometimes both are true (as
with *prime* and *exactly two factors* — which is why that pair makes a definition), and sometimes only one
is (as with $x=3$ and $x^2=9$). So when a question asks *"is this the same statement?"*, the answer never
comes from checking truth — it comes from **comparing the arrows**.

**When both directions are true**, you may join them into a single "if and only if", and that is what a
mathematical **definition** usually is: *"$n$ is prime **iff** $n$ has exactly two positive factors."*
:::

# Part 3 — Hard

Real Paper 2 material. Both of these are the standard question types built directly on Arg1.

## Question 6

::: {.question}
In this question, $k$ is a positive integer. Consider the theorem
$$\text{If } 2^k + 1 \text{ is a prime, then } k \text{ is a power of } 2. \tag{$*$}$$

Which of the following statements, **taken individually**, is/are equivalent to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; If $k$ is a power of $2$, then $2^k+1$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $2^k+1$ is not prime **only if** $k$ is not a power of $2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; A **sufficient** condition for $k$ to be a power of $2$ is that $2^k+1$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I, II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** I and II &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** I and III &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** I only &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** II only &nbsp;&nbsp; **G** III only
&nbsp;&nbsp; **H** None
:::

Do not think about primes at all — this question is about **shape**. The first move, and it takes ten
seconds, is to [give the two halves names]{.hl} and write $(*)$ as a single arrow. Then translate each of
I, II, III into an arrow by the rules and compare. Statement II is the one designed to catch you: it has
negations on both sides so it *smells* like a contrapositive, and you must check whether the arrow was
actually reversed as well.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — deciding which rephrasings are equivalent to a given theorem *(2023 Paper 2, Q11)*
:::


Name the halves: let $P$ = "$2^k+1$ is prime" and $Q$ = "$k$ is a power of $2$". Then

$$(*) \;=\; P \Rightarrow Q .$$

**I.** "If $k$ is a power of $2$, then $2^k+1$ is prime" is $Q \Rightarrow P$ — the arrow the wrong way
round, i.e. the **converse**. Not equivalent. → **No**

**II.** Apply the rule: "$A$ **only if** $B$" is $A \Rightarrow B$, with $A = \text{not } P$ and
$B = \text{not } Q$. So statement II is
$$\text{not } P \Rightarrow \text{not } Q .$$
Now compare. The contrapositive of $(*)$ is $\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P$ — negated **and**
reversed. Statement II has [negated both halves but left the arrow pointing the same way]{.hl}, so it is
the contrapositive of $Q \Rightarrow P$, i.e. of statement **I** — the converse again. Not equivalent to
$(*)$. → **No**

**III.** "A sufficient condition for $Q$ is $P$" means $P$ is enough to force $Q$, that is
$P \Rightarrow Q$ — which is $(*)$ word for word. → **Yes**

**Answer: G (III only).** $\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Marking II equivalent because "both halves are negated" | The contrapositive needs **negate *and* reverse**. Negating alone gives you the *converse's* contrapositive. |
| Marking I equivalent | $Q\Rightarrow P$ is the converse; a statement and its converse are not equivalent. |
| Trying to decide whether $(*)$ is actually true | Irrelevant. You are asked which statements **say the same thing**, not which are true. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the naming trick, and the four related statements

**Always name the halves first.** Writing $P$ and $Q$ on your paper converts a wordy question into arrows
you can compare at a glance, and it removes the temptation to reason about the mathematics (primes, powers
of 2) which is entirely beside the point.

From any statement $P \Rightarrow Q$ there are four related sentences, and only one is equivalent:

| Name | Form | Equivalent to $P \Rightarrow Q$? |
|---|---|---|
| **Original** | $P \Rightarrow Q$ | — |
| **Converse** | $Q \Rightarrow P$ | **No** |
| **Inverse** | $\text{not } P \Rightarrow \text{not } Q$ | **No** (it is the converse's contrapositive) |
| **Contrapositive** | $\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P$ | **Yes, always** |

Statement II above is the **inverse**, dressed in "only if" so that it looks like a contrapositive. This is
a standard TMUA move: *negation is not enough — the arrow must turn round too.*

**"Sufficient" and "necessary"** (Session 3, but you need them here):

- "$P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$" $\;=\; P \Rightarrow Q$ — $P$ is enough on its own.
- "$P$ is **necessary** for $Q$" $\;=\; Q \Rightarrow P$ — you can't have $Q$ without $P$.
:::

## Question 7

::: {.question}
Here is an attempt to solve the inequality $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 < 0$.

> $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 < 0$
> **I** &nbsp; if and only if &nbsp; $(x^2-1)(x^2-4) < 0$
> **II** &nbsp; if and only if &nbsp; $1 < x^2 < 4$
> **III** &nbsp; if and only if &nbsp; $1 < x < 2$

Which of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The argument is completely correct. &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** The first error is in line I.
&nbsp;&nbsp; **C** The first error is in line II. &nbsp;&nbsp; **D** The first error is in line III.
:::

Go **line by line**, and at each line ask exactly one question: [does this step run both ways?]{.hl} It is
not enough that the line follows *from* the previous one — an "if and only if" claims the reverse as well.
Watch particularly for the classic one-way moves: squaring, square-rooting, multiplying by something that
might be negative or zero, and quietly dropping a case.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a chain of "if and only if" steps; finding the first line that is not reversible
:::


**Line I.** Factorising: $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = (x^2-1)(x^2-4)$. This is an **identity** — the two expressions
are the same number for every $x$ — so the step is reversible. ✓

**Line II.** This one claims $(x^2-1)(x^2-4) < 0 \iff 1 < x^2 < 4$, so — since the whole question is about
reversibility — [check both directions explicitly]{.hl}.

**($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $(x^2-1)(x^2-4) < 0$.** A product is negative exactly when the two factors have
**opposite signs**, so there are two cases:

| Case | Conditions | Result |
|---|---|---|
| ① | $x^2-1 > 0$ and $x^2-4 < 0$ | $1 < x^2 < 4$ ✓ |
| ② | $x^2-1 < 0$ and $x^2-4 > 0$ | $x^2 < 1$ **and** $x^2 > 4$ — **impossible** |

Case ② cannot happen (no number is both less than $1$ and greater than $4$), so case ① is forced and
$1 < x^2 < 4$. ✓

*Shortcut worth knowing: $x^2 - 1$ is always **bigger** than $x^2 - 4$, so the bigger one cannot be the
negative one. That kills case ② instantly.*

**($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $1 < x^2 < 4$.** Then $x^2 - 1 > 0$ and $x^2 - 4 < 0$, so

$$(x^2-1)(x^2-4) = (\text{positive}) \times (\text{negative}) < 0 . \qquad ✓$$

Both directions hold, so line II genuinely is an "if and only if". ✓

**Line III.** Here is the error — and notice it is found by doing exactly what we just did for line II,
checking each direction separately.

**($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $1 < x < 2$.** Then squaring (legitimate here, since everything is positive)
gives $1 < x^2 < 4$. ✓ &nbsp; *This direction is fine, which is why the line looks convincing.*

**($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $1 < x^2 < 4$.** Does $1 < x < 2$ follow? **No** — because
[$x$ may be negative]{.hl}. Take $x = -1.5$: then $x^2 = 2.25$, so line II holds, but $-1.5$ does not
satisfy $1 < x < 2$. ✗

So **one direction survives and the other fails**, which means the two lines are *not* equivalent and the
claimed "if and only if" is false. The correct conclusion is

$$1 < |x| < 2, \qquad \text{that is} \qquad 1 < x < 2 \;\text{ or }\; -2 < x < -1 .$$

**Answer: D — the first error is in line III.** $\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Answering **A** | Every line *looked* fine going forwards; line III fails going **backwards**, which is what "iff" also claims. |
| Answering **C**, thinking line II drops a case | Line II is genuinely two-sided and correct. Check before you accuse a line. |
| $\sqrt{x^2} = x$ | $\sqrt{x^2} = \lvert x\rvert$. This single fact is what line III gets wrong. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — attacking a chain, and the one-way moves

**Method.**

1. Go **line by line**; never skim to the end.
2. At each line, **check the two directions separately**. Write them out:
   - **($\Rightarrow$)** assume the previous line, derive this one;
   - **($\Leftarrow$)** assume this line, derive the previous one.
3. The moment a line fails in **either** direction, **stop** — you were asked for the *first* error.
4. If every line survives both directions, "completely correct" really is the answer. That option is
   **not** a decoy.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Step 2 is where people lose this question**, and it is subtle: the forwards direction is usually the
obvious one, so a false line still *reads* perfectly well. Line III above is exactly that — going
backwards ($1<x<2 \Rightarrow 1<x^2<4$) is flawless, and only the forwards direction breaks.

So a line is **not** verified just because you can get to it. Ask explicitly: *can I get back?*
:::

**The moves that are one-way** (these are where chains break):

| Move | Why it can fail |
|---|---|
| **Squaring** both sides | $x = -2 \Rightarrow x^2 = 4$, but $x^2 = 4 \not\Rightarrow x = -2$ |
| **Square-rooting** | $\sqrt{x^2} = \lvert x \rvert$, not $x$ — the negative branch is lost |
| **Multiplying** both sides by an expression | Fine only if it is known **non-zero** (and sign-fixed, for inequalities) |
| **Cancelling** a common factor | From $ab = ac$ you may **not** deduce $b=c$ — unless $a \ne 0$ |
| **Dropping half** of a two-sided inequality | $-2 < u < 2$ becoming $u < 2$ loses cases *unless* the other half is automatic |

That last row deserves a warning: dropping half an inequality is **sometimes legitimate**. If the discarded
half is always true anyway — for instance $-2 < x^2 - 1$ holds for every real $x$, because $x^2 \ge 0$ —
then nothing is lost and the step is fine. So do not pattern-match; **check whether the discarded condition
was doing any work.**
:::

# Part 4 — Exam bank

Four from real exam material. Three of them share a format the TMUA loves and nothing else does:
**"given that exactly one of these statements is true, which one is it?"** You are told almost nothing about
the mathematics — the answer comes from the *shapes* of the statements alone.

::: {.callout-important}
## The trick that solves "exactly one is true"

Translate every option into $\Rightarrow$ form. Then use one idea:

> **If option $X$ being true would force option $Y$ to be true as well, then $X$ cannot be the answer** —
> because then *two* statements would be true, and you were promised exactly one.

So eliminate every option that **implies another option**, or that is **equivalent to another option** (two
equivalent options stand or fall together, so neither can be the unique one). What survives is the answer.
*You never need to know what the underlying statement actually says.*
:::

---

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set B · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the four options below about a particular statement $S$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $S$ is true **if** $x^{2}<1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $S$ is true **if and only if** $x^{2}<1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $S$ is true **if** $x^{2}<2$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $S$ is true **if and only if** $x^{2}<2$.

Given that **exactly one** of these options is correct, which one is it?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — no mathematics required at all)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** Translate all four, remembering that "$S$ **if** $H$" means $H\Rightarrow S$:

| | Option | In arrows |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | true if $x^{2}<1$ | $x^{2}<1\Rightarrow S$ |
| **B** | true iff $x^{2}<1$ | $x^{2}<1\Leftrightarrow S$ |
| **C** | true if $x^{2}<2$ | $x^{2}<2\Rightarrow S$ |
| **D** | true iff $x^{2}<2$ | $x^{2}<2\Leftrightarrow S$ |

Now chase the implications between the *options*:

- **B $\Rightarrow$ A**: an "if and only if" contains the "if". So if B were correct, A would be correct too.
- **D $\Rightarrow$ C**: same reason.
- **C $\Rightarrow$ A**: because $x^{2}<1$ is a *stronger* condition than $x^{2}<2$. If every $x$ with
  $x^{2}<2$ makes $S$ true, then certainly every $x$ with $x^{2}<1$ does.

So $D\Rightarrow C\Rightarrow A$ and $B\Rightarrow A$: **each of B, C, D would drag A along with it**, giving
two correct options. Only **A** can stand alone. $\;\blacksquare$

*Note what was never needed:* we never asked what $S$ is. The question is pure Session-1 translation plus one
observation about which conditions are stronger.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}

:::

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
$f$ is a function and $a$ is a real number. Given that **exactly one** of the following statements is true,
which one is it?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a\le0$ **only if** $f(a)\le0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(a)>0$ **if** $a>0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(a)>0$ is **sufficient** for $a>0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(a)\le0$ is **necessary** for $a\le0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** **If** $f(a)>0$ **then** $a>0$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $a>0$ **if** $f(a)>0$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — five of the six say the same thing)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**B.** Write $P$ for "$a>0$" and $Q$ for "$f(a)>0$". *Note that "$a\le0$" is exactly $\lnot P$ and
"$f(a)\le0$" is exactly $\lnot Q$* — the question is built on that.

| | Option | Literally | Simplified |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | $\lnot P$ only if $\lnot Q$ | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |
| **B** | $Q$ if $P$ | $P\Rightarrow Q$ | $\mathbf{P\Rightarrow Q}$ |
| **C** | $Q$ sufficient for $P$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |
| **D** | $\lnot Q$ necessary for $\lnot P$ | $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |
| **E** | if $Q$ then $P$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |
| **F** | $P$ if $Q$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ | $Q\Rightarrow P$ |

**Five options — A, C, D, E, F — are the identical statement $Q\Rightarrow P$**, written five different ways:
as a contrapositive (A, D), as "sufficient" (C), as "if…then" (E) and as a reversed "if" (F). They are all
true together or all false together, so **none of them can be the unique true one**.

That leaves **B**, the only option pointing the other way. $\;\blacksquare$

*This question is the entire session compressed into one item.* Every translation rule from Part 1 appears
once, and the reward for knowing them is that you answer in twenty seconds without touching $f$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Let $P$ be a property of a real number $x$. Each of the following is a statement about **all** real values of
$x$. **Exactly one** of the following statements is true. Which one is it?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** If $\lvert x\rvert<1$, then $P$ is true.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** If $\lvert x\rvert<2$, then $P$ is true.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** If $P$ is true, then $\lvert x\rvert<1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** If $P$ is true, then $\lvert x\rvert<2$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** If $P$ is not true, then $x^{2}\ge1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** If $P$ is not true, then $x^{2}\ge4$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $P$ is true **only if** $x^{2}<1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — pair off the duplicates, then rank what is left)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D.** First notice that $x^{2}<1\iff\lvert x\rvert<1$ and $x^{2}<4\iff\lvert x\rvert<2$, so options
**E**, **F** and **G** are not new statements at all:

- **E** is $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lvert x\rvert\ge1$, the **contrapositive of A** — so **A and E are
  equivalent**, and neither can be the unique one.
- **F** is the **contrapositive of B** — so **B and F are equivalent**, and neither can be unique.
- **G** is "$P$ only if $x^{2}<1$", i.e. $P\Rightarrow\lvert x\rvert<1$ — the **same statement as C**, so
  neither C nor G can be unique.

That removes five options at a stroke and leaves only **B**'s pair and **D**. Now rank the survivors:

- **B $\Rightarrow$ A**: if $P$ holds for every $x$ with $\lvert x\rvert<2$, it certainly holds on the
  smaller set $\lvert x\rvert<1$. So B would make A true as well — **B is out**.
- **C $\Rightarrow$ D**: if $P$ forces $\lvert x\rvert<1$, it forces $\lvert x\rvert<2$ too. So C would
  make D true as well — **C is out**, which we already knew.

**D** implies none of the others, and nothing else survives. $\;\blacksquare$

**The two moves to carry into the exam.** *One:* a statement and its contrapositive are the same statement,
so an option paired with its own contrapositive is automatically eliminated. *Two:* between two "if $H$ then
$P$" options, the one with the **wider** $H$ is stronger; between two "if $P$ then $C$" options, the one with
the **narrower** $C$ is stronger. The unique truth is always the **weakest** surviving statement.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}

:::

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
The equation $\;\sin x\left(1-\cos^{2}x\right)=k\sin x\;$ has exactly $n$ distinct solutions in
$[0,2\pi]$, where $k$ is a real constant. Which of the following statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $0<k<1$ **if** $n=7$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $n=3$ **only if** $k<0$ or $k>1$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $n=5$ and $k\neq1$ **cannot both** be true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp; **D** I and III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** II and III only &nbsp; **G** all three &nbsp; **H** none of them
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — do the maths once, then read off three statement forms)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D.** *Do not divide by $\sin x$* — factorise:
$$\sin x\left(1-\cos^{2}x\right)-k\sin x=0\;\Longrightarrow\;\sin x\left(\sin^{2}x-k\right)=0 .$$

$\sin x=0$ gives $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ — **three solutions, always**. The rest come from $\sin^{2}x=k$:

| $k$ | extra solutions from $\sin^{2}x=k$ | total $n$ |
|---|---|---|
| $k<0$ | none | $3$ |
| $k=0$ | $x=0,\pi,2\pi$ — **already counted** | $3$ |
| $0<k<1$ | four ($\sin x=\pm\sqrt k$, two each) | $7$ |
| $k=1$ | $x=\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac{3\pi}2$ | $5$ |
| $k>1$ | none | $3$ |

So $\;n=7\iff0<k<1$, $\;n=5\iff k=1$, $\;n=3\iff k\le0$ or $k>1$.

Now translate the three statements:

- **I** — "$0<k<1$ **if** $n=7$" means $n=7\Rightarrow0<k<1$. **True ✓**
- **II** — "$n=3$ **only if** $k<0$ or $k>1$" means $n=3\Rightarrow(k<0$ or $k>1)$. **False ✗** —
  *$k=0$ also gives $n=3$*, and $k=0$ satisfies neither $k<0$ nor $k>1$. The condition offered is not
  necessary.
- **III** — "$n=5$ and $k\neq1$ cannot both be true" says $n=5\Rightarrow k=1$. **True ✓**

I and III only. $\;\blacksquare$

**Two traps, both from Session 1.** *"$A$ if $B$" is $B\Rightarrow A$* — statement I points backwards from
the way it reads. And *"cannot both be true" is an implication in disguise*: "not ($X$ and $\lnot Y$)" is
exactly $X\Rightarrow Y$. The single boundary case $k=0$ decides statement II.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}

:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q14 &nbsp;◆</span>

::: {.question}
Three lines are given by
$$ax+by+c=0,\qquad bx+cy+a=0,\qquad cx+ay+b=0,$$
where $a,b,c$ are non-zero reals. Which **one** of the following is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** if two of the lines are parallel, then all three are parallel.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** if two of the lines are parallel, then the third is perpendicular to the other two.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** if two of the lines are parallel, then the third is parallel to $y=x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** if two of the lines are parallel, then the third is perpendicular to $y=x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** if two of the lines are perpendicular, then all three meet at a point.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** if two of the lines are perpendicular, then the third is parallel to $y=x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** if two of the lines are perpendicular, then the third is perpendicular to $y=x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a real TMUA question; find the invariant first)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**F.** Seven options, each an implication — *do not test them one by one.* Find the one fact that is true of
**every** such triple of lines, and all seven answers fall out of it.

**The invariant.** The gradients are
$$m_{1}=-\frac ab,\qquad m_{2}=-\frac bc,\qquad m_{3}=-\frac ca,$$
and their product collapses:
$$m_{1}m_{2}m_{3}=\left(-\frac ab\right)\left(-\frac bc\right)\left(-\frac ca\right)=-\frac{abc}{abc}=-1 .$$
*Whatever $a,b,c$ are, the three gradients multiply to $-1$.*

**Now read each hypothesis off the invariant.**

- **If two are perpendicular** — say $m_{1}m_{2}=-1$ — then $m_{3}=\dfrac{-1}{m_{1}m_{2}}=\dfrac{-1}{-1}=1$.
  Gradient $1$ is exactly "parallel to $y=x$". **F is true**, and **G** (which wants $m_{3}=-1$) is false.
- **If two are parallel** — say $m_{1}=m_{2}=m$ — then $m^{2}m_{3}=-1$, so $m_{3}=-\dfrac{1}{m^{2}}$, which
  is **always negative**. That single observation kills **C** at once (it needs $m_{3}=1>0$), and the rest
  fail because $m_{3}$ is *not determined*: with $m=-\tfrac12$ the third gradient is $-4$, with $m=-1$ it is
  $-1$, with $m=-2$ it is $-\tfrac14$. So the third line is sometimes parallel to the other two and sometimes
  not (**A**), sometimes perpendicular to them and sometimes not (**B**), sometimes of gradient $-1$ and
  sometimes not (**D**).
- **E** claims concurrency. The three lines meet at a point exactly when
  $\begin{vmatrix}a&b&c\\ b&c&a\\ c&a&b\end{vmatrix}=0$, i.e. when $a+b+c=0$ (or $a=b=c$) — a condition about
  the coefficients that perpendicularity does nothing to force. *Counterexample:* $a=b=-6,\ c=6$ makes two of
  the lines perpendicular, yet $a+b+c=-6\neq0$, so they are not concurrent. **E is false.**

**The habit worth taking.** When every option is an implication with the *same* hypothesis, the question is
really asking *"what is determined by that hypothesis?"* — so compute that one quantity and compare. Here one
line of algebra ($m_{1}m_{2}m_{3}=-1$) decided all seven. $\;\blacksquare$

*Gradients, perpendicularity and concurrency are Paper 1 material — see the
**[coordinate geometry clinic](../lessons/coordinate_geometry_clinic/class_material.qmd)**. This question is
a reminder that Paper 2 wraps Paper 1 content in a logical shell.*
:::

Working
:::
